start-kit-posture-warmup.summary: Start with a small kit, a way of sitting and holding the pencil that lets long lines come from the shoulder, and a five-minute warm-up you can run before any session. One pencil, one fineliner, an eraser, cheap printer paper and a sketchbook you are happy to fill with bad drawings are enough for months. The warm-up stays short on purpose so it never replaces the session.
learning_outcomes: Run a five-minute warm-up before a session and keep it to about a quarter of the session time

practice.title: Optional: posture photo check
practice.description: Prop your phone up to the side and record a minute of yourself drawing. Check whether your ears are over your shoulders, your wrist is neutral and you are leaning into the paper. Change one thing and record again.

done_when.text: Timed with a phone, you can sit down and make the first mark within one minute
You have a written five-minute warm-up and a 90-second version, and you have run the warm-up before six sessions, any spacing

revisit.title: Cold warm-up and long line
revisit.description: With the module closed, run your warm-up from memory, then draw five lines about as long as your forearm between dots placed somewhere new on the page, from the shoulder. Check the wrist stayed quiet and that you rotated the paper for the awkward direction.

found-practice-method.summary: Short sessions with one focus, spread over the week, work better than long irregular ones. This module sets the session shape used throughout the app (warm-up, one revisit, one focused drill, a quick check, stop on time), a sketchbook kept as a record rather than a gallery, and the habit of redrawing what you learnt from memory a few days later. Progress is counted in totals, never in streaks.

resources.notes: Proko's two-week challenge: a page of line drawings from life per day, a minute of looking first, 5 to 30 minutes per drawing. Use its page format; here the count matters, not consecutive days.

practice.description: Choose three to five short sessions a week and put them in your calendar with a start time. Give each a single focus from your current modules. Keep them short enough to finish on tired days, and keep Tuesday and Thursday for short optional sessions only.

practice.title: Twenty dated pages
practice.description: Fill twenty sketchbook pages with line drawings from life, any spacing, each dated. Look at the subject for a minute before drawing and spend 5 to 30 minutes per drawing. Proko's two-week challenge asks for a page a day; here a missed day resets nothing.

done_when.text: You have completed 12 planned sessions, any spacing, each with one stated focus and a planned stop
You have at least 20 dated sketchbook pages, any spacing, and the pages you dislike are still in the book
You have redrawn one exercise from memory on three separate days and compared each attempt with the original

revisit.title: Name the gap, pick the drill
revisit.description: Take the last drawing you made in any module. With this module closed, write which single skill let it down most and the one drill you will do next session, then run that drill for five minutes on a new subject.

baseline-imagination-check.summary: Draw the same ten subjects from imagination, five to ten minutes each, with no reference: a person running, a dog, a chair, a car, a tree, a room, a street corner, a hand holding a cup, a face looking up and an invented creature. Photograph the set and keep it as drawn. You draw the identical set again at every phase benchmark, so the gallery shows your drawing from imagination changing side by side.
learning_outcomes: Draw each of the ten baseline subjects from imagination in 5 to 10 minutes without reference
Name, for each drawing, the one thing you had to guess
Compare two sets and say what changed in construction, proportion and clarity
Use the list of guesses to choose what to study next

resources.notes: Optional, after your first set: Peter Han builds an invented character from stored structure and talks through his decisions. Watch it after the baseline, not before, so the baseline stays a true record.
A short explanation of a visual library: collect references by subject, study from life, test recall without reference, vary the viewpoint. It is the method behind the gaps your baseline shows.

practice.title: Draw the ten
practice.description: Set a timer for 7 minutes per subject (5 minimum, 10 maximum). Draw each subject on its own half page, no reference and no erasing, in this order: a person running, a dog, a chair, a car, a tree, a room, a street corner, a hand holding a cup, a face looking up, an invented creature.
practice.dose: 10 drawings, 5 to 10 min each, one or two sittings

practice.title: Mark what you guessed
practice.description: Beside each drawing write one line naming what you had to guess, for example how the knee bends when running, the shape of a car's wheel arch or where the ear sits on a tilted head. This list is a map of what to study, not a score.

practice.title: Check three against photos, afterwards
practice.description: Only after the set is photographed, look up a photo for three of the subjects and write the biggest structural difference for each. Do not redraw the baseline; it stays as drawn.

practice.title: Side by side at each benchmark
practice.description: When a benchmark asks for the set again, draw all ten the same way, then lay the new photo beside the earlier ones and write one sentence per subject: what is clearer now and what is still guessed.

done_when.text: All ten subjects are drawn from imagination, each within 5 to 10 minutes, with no reference open
The set is photographed and dated as one record where the benchmarks can find it
Each drawing has a one-line note naming what you guessed
For three subjects you can point to the biggest structural difference between your drawing and a photo

common_mistakes: Looking up reference during the set, which turns a measure of imagination into a copy
Polishing one drawing for half an hour and skipping others; the time limit is part of the test
Redrawing the baseline later to make it look better; it is a record, so keep it as drawn
Changing the ten prompts between sets, which makes the comparison meaningless

revisit.title: One baseline subject, cold
revisit.description: Pick one of the ten subjects at random and draw it from imagination in 5 minutes, without looking at your earlier set. Then compare it with your baseline drawing and with one photo, and name the biggest structural difference.
